name: Akuriyó
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Meira, Sérgio. 1998. A reconstruction of Proto-Taranoan: phonology and inflectional morphology. MA thesis, Rice University, Houston. xiii+199 pp. (UMI 1389108; hdl 1911/17197)
catalog_locator: Chapter 3, pp. 18-19 with footnote 2; support: p. 56 and pp. 79-80.
catalog_quote: Tiriyó has a rhythmic stress system based on the predictable alternation of stressed and unstressed syllables, with stress being realized as vowel length and high pitch (cf. Meira ms-a for a details). Words composed only of (C)V (i.e. light) syllables follow this pattern rigorously (e.g. /amatakana/ 'bird sp.', /kɨtapotomapoti/ 'we (all) will make him / her help', pronounced as [a.má:.ta.ká:.na], [kɨ.tá:.po.tó:.ma.pó:.ti]), with the restriction that the last syllable can never bear stress (e.g. /siririme/ 'blue', pronounced as [si.rí:.ri.me], not *[si.rí:.ri.mé:]). Words containing a non-(C)V (i.e. heavy) syllable deviate from this pattern in that the heavy syllable is obligatorily stressed, with the rhythmic pattern resuming after it (e.g. /wempakane/, pronounced [wém.pa.ká:.ne], not *[wem.pá:.ka.ne]. ...). This pattern of stress assignment is called iambic (cf. Hayes 1995 ...). Akuriyó appears to have a similar system, with glottalization often taking the place of, and sometimes co-occurring with, vowel length; the glottal stops which seem to be expressing stress will be written as superscripts. Not all glottals result from rhythmic stress, though (cf. 4.2.2). [fn. 2] In Akuriyó, an automatic syllable-final glottal stop seems to be part of the rhythmic stress system; it frequently occurred as the main corelate of secondary stress, corresponding to vowel lengthening in Tiriyó. These glottal stops, which can precede any consonant, have not been considered here.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.rule_in_words: Akuriyó is described (tentatively: 'appears to have') as sharing Tiriyó's iambic rhythmic stress: counting from the left edge, every second light (C)V syllable is stressed (realized as vowel length/high pitch in Tiriyó; in Akuriyó often as a syllable-final glottal stop instead of or alongside length), heavy (non-CV) syllables are always stressed with the count restarting after them, and the word-final syllable is never stressed. No single primary-stress position is singled out; the system is quantity-sensitive alternating rhythm rather than a fixed syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: The alternating rhythmic beats are the system itself; fn.2 says the Akuriyó syllable-final glottal stop 'frequently occurred as the main corelate of secondary stress, corresponding to vowel lengthening in Tiriyó'. No separate statement distinguishing a primary stress from the rhythmic secondaries in Akuriyó.
new_statements.exceptions: Final syllable never stressed (stated for Tiriyó, system said to be shared). 'Not all glottals result from rhythmic stress' (p.19; some Akuriyó glottal stops are segmental reflexes of PT *c, cf. 4.2.2, 5.3). pp.79-80: first-person possessed forms of consonant-initial nouns carry a long first root vowel (mo:ta-rï 'my shoulder' vs mota), analysed as a fossil of iambic stress after loss of a syllabic prefix -- i.e. a morphologically conditioned initial length/stress. Author flags all Akuriyó conclusions as preliminary (few days of data, heavy Tiriyó contact influence, p.5-6, p.16).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rhythmic stress inferred from elicited words/paradigms in field notes (Meira 1997 at Tepoe with native speakers Onore and Maraiaimë; Gildea 1995 with a non-native speaker). The explicit rule is stated for Tiriyó and extended to Akuriyó by 'appears to have a similar system'; hedged, not an independent full analysis. No phrase-level discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: Meira's 'Akuriyó' = Glottolog akur1238 Akurio (ISO ako), the Taranoan language of the group contacted 1968-71 and resettled at Tepoe/Pelelu Tepu, Suriname; data from native speakers at Tepoe (1997) and one non-native speaker at Missão Tiriós, Brazil (1995). De Goeje's 1909 'Wama' list is treated by Meira as early Akuriyó. Not to be confused with Tiriyó (trio1238), whose stress rule is the one stated explicitly and extended to Akuriyó by analogy; author warns Akuriyó data may be Tiriyó-influenced.

sources.note: Family-level: many Cariban languages have rhythmic (iambic) stress (Table 1 illustrates Tiriyó; cites Meira 1998), some have cumulative penultimate stress (Panare, Bakairi, Kuikuro, Yukpa). Akuriyó appears only on the map; no Akuriyó-specific stress statement.
